ultherapy-hifu-skin-tightening.text: Users have this clinic treatment to lift loose skin under the chin, along the jawline and on the brow, aiming for a sharper lower-face contour without surgery. Results appear gradually over a few months. Support comes from small device studies and regulatory clearance for brow, neck and chest lifting.

thermage-monopolar-rf.text: Thermage is used in clinics to tighten mild-to-moderate skin laxity on the face, neck and eyelids, so skin looks firmer and fine lines look softer. Gradual results are reported in small studies, which is where the evidence for this appearance use currently sits.

profhilo-skin-booster-injectables.text: Profhilo and similar skin boosters are used to improve skin quality, giving a more hydrated, supple and smoother-looking complexion rather than added volume. Small studies report gains in hydration and elasticity, and the products are generally positioned as complements to fillers.

rejuran-salmon-dna-facial.text: Rejuran and other salmon DNA (PN or PDRN) facials are promoted for skin texture, fine lines and under-eye skin quality, as an alternative to volume fillers. Popularity has run ahead of published data, and the evidence for this appearance use is still thin.

chain: Better texture, fewer fine lines and scars
prp-facial-vampire-facial.text: Users have PRP facials, popularly the vampire facial, for rejuvenated skin, smoother texture, fine lines and acne scars. Some do-it-yourself communities also try home versions. Small studies exist for skin rejuvenation, though controlled evidence for facial appearance is limited.

chain: Local effect on skin, hair or fat
Fuller hair, fresher skin, less fat
mesotherapy.text: Mesotherapy is used to inject vitamin and drug cocktails for hair thickening, skin rejuvenation and local fat reduction. Small studies back some uses, such as scalp treatment, while cocktails vary widely and appearance claims for fat and skin remain largely untested.

chain: Light pulses target pigment and vessels
ipl-photofacial.text: IPL photofacials are used to fade sun spots, uneven pigmentation, redness and visible small blood vessels for a clearer, more even complexion. Support is strongest for pigment and vascular concerns, and weaker for wrinkles.

plasma-pen-fibroblasting.text: Plasma pens are promoted for tightening loose eyelid skin, smoothing lines and removing small blemishes, with cheaper home devices sold as clinic substitutes. Controlled trials for cosmetic tightening were not found, so the appearance benefit rests on provider and user reports.

chain: Less downward pull on lower face
platysma-botox-nefertiti-lift.text: Users have botulinum toxin injected along the jawline and neck bands to soften platysmal cords and give a subtle lift and sharper lower-face contour. Case series and small trials describe the effect, which is temporary and modest.

chain: Light suction moves skin and fluid
facial-cupping.text: Facial cupping is a self-care ritual in which small suction cups are glided over the face to lift, tone and depuff. People report a temporary flushed, fresher look. Face-specific research is nearly absent, so lasting lifting remains a belief.

face-taping-frownies-sleep-patches.text: Users wear paper or tape patches overnight on the forehead, between the brows and around the eyes and mouth to soften expression lines. Frownies has sold them for over a century. Published trials are absent, so the benefit rests on anecdote.

lymphatic-drainage-facial-massage.text: Users massage the face and neck lightly, by hand or with tools, to reduce puffiness and get a more defined, depuffed look. The manual technique is established in clinical settings, while cosmetic facial evidence is absent.

chain: Estriol acts on skin estrogen receptors
topical-estrogen-estriol-cream.text: Estriol cream is discussed for thicker, firmer, smoother skin, mostly among older users. It is an off-label use of a menopausal hormone therapy ingredient. Skin data exist in menopausal women, while data for appearance use in general are thin.

topical-rapamycin.text: Longevity-minded users apply rapamycin cream hoping to slow visible skin aging. It is an off-label use, since topical forms are approved for a rare facial condition. One small exploratory aging trial exists.

chain: Better skin blood flow and collagen
quit-smoking-vaping.text: Quitting tobacco or vaping is cited to avoid or reduce smoker's face, with its wrinkles, sagging and dull yellowish complexion. The link between smoking and facial aging is observational, and trials of quitting for appearance are missing.

sleeping-on-your-back.text: Some looksmaxxing practitioners sleep face-up to avoid sleep lines caused by pressing the face into a pillow for hours. The idea is based on anecdote and plausible mechanics, and the wrinkle benefit has not been tested in trials.

bee-venom-snake-peptide-syn-ake-creams.text: Syn-Ake and bee venom creams are sold as topical alternatives to Botox for smoothing expression lines. The reasoning is that a peptide mimics a venom compound and relaxes muscle. Evidence so far consists of laboratory data.

sunscreen-maxxing.text: Sunscreen-maxxing means strict daily SPF use with regular reapplication to limit UV-driven skin aging. It is regarded as the best-evidenced anti-photoaging habit in the wiki's sources, with studies showing less visible skin aging in regular users.

chain: Collagen builds, pores and spots improve
tretinoin-protocol-tret-buffering.text: Looksmaxxing forums share routines for starting tretinoin slowly and buffering it with moisturiser to reduce irritation, aiming for smoother, clearer, less wrinkled skin. Tretinoin itself is well studied for acne and photoaging, while the buffering routine is not.

hydrogen-water-topical-hydrogen.text: Hydrogen water and hydrogen skincare are promoted in wellness and anti-aging circles for antioxidant effects on skin. Users hope for a fresher, younger complexion. The evidence for appearance benefits is thin.

placenta-sheep-placenta-creams.text: Sheep placenta creams are marketed for skin regeneration, moisture and fewer wrinkles. Users buy them as an anti-aging step in a routine. No clinical evidence for the appearance claims was found.

chain: Laser light absorbed by blood vessels
pulsed-dye-laser-v-beam-for-redness.text: Pulsed dye lasers such as the Vbeam are used in clinics to reduce facial redness, broken capillaries and rosacea-related flushing. The technology is long established for birthmarks and vascular lesions. Temporary bruising is common after treatment.

hydrafacial.text: Hydrafacial is a clinic facial that cleanses, exfoliates, extracts and applies serums, giving a fresher, brighter, smoother look right after treatment with little downtime. The immediate glow is visible, while the published evidence base is small.

metronidazole-ivermectin-rosacea-creams.text: Prescription metronidazole and ivermectin creams are used to calm the bumps and inflammation of rosacea for a clearer, less irritated face. Clinicians consider them well studied for that purpose, though they do little for persistent flat redness.

brimonidine-gel-mirvaso.text: Brimonidine gel is a prescription product used for persistent facial redness in rosacea, reducing visible flushing within hours. The effect is temporary and the product has a 2013 FDA approval for this use. Rebound redness has been reported in some users.

oxymetazoline-cream-rhofade.text: Oxymetazoline cream (Rhofade) is a prescription vasoconstrictor approved in 2017 for persistent facial redness in rosacea. It narrows vessels to reduce visible redness for a temporary, more even-looking complexion.

glass-skin-routine.text: Glass skin is a K-beauty ideal of smooth, translucent, dewy skin, pursued through a multi-step routine of cleansing, hydrating and exfoliating. It is as much an aesthetic goal as a defined protocol, and no dedicated clinical studies exist.

chain: Lower blood sugar and insulin spikes
low-glycemic-anti-inflammatory-diet.text: Users favour low-GI foods and cut sugar, and sometimes dairy, aiming for clearer skin and less redness or puffiness. Trials are encouraging for glycemic load and acne, while a full anti-inflammatory diet is untested for appearance.

chain: Heat and steam warm the skin
facial-steaming-sauna.text: People use facial steaming and sauna sessions for a flushed, hydrated, cleansed-looking glow. Sauna has health research in other areas, and nothing on facial appearance has been studied.

hydration-water-chugging.text: Skincare and appearance communities suggest drinking large amounts of water, sometimes gallons a day, for plumper, glowy skin and less face puffiness. Trials have not tested this appearance claim.
